comments:
I'm not a super-fan of the 7 successive caps of KMACXOF.  KmacXof would be the next-most-reasonable, but would be asserting that we think "Kmac128" is a reasonable name... which I'm not sure it is.

Otherwise, it seems reasonable to me.  Especially the differentiation for if we can ever add the streaming semantics of "squeeze" to the XOFs.
Given that we called SHAKE in .NET 8 `Shake128` and not `SHAKE128`, and `KMACXOF` is a bit alphabet soup, I am leaning toward `Kmac128` and `KmacXof128`.
This is on hold pending some input from the Windows team about the CNG implementation.
We have a path forward on Windows now, so going back to 9.0.

review_comments: Referencing one KMAC will keep both fields rooted in AoT.  That's probably small enough to be fine, but again there's an "at some point we will need to rethink this".
Yeah. Fixing rooting for AOT deep in our abstractions is bigger than KMAC. I'm not sure its worth it either, and it would force pushing abstractions all the way up to the public API surface.
I don't think these size limits were documented, either.

Yeah. This PR actually has the beginnings of trying to pull the Android and OpenSSL apart because it is untenable to have Android keep pretending it can be OpenSSL.

HashProviderDispenser.Unix is not actually a new file, Git is just a little confused what is going on.

HashProviderDispenser.OpenSsl and HashProviderDispenser.Android are new. The .Unix one is shared between Android and OpenSsl. I could fully split the two and have no code sharing, but it would be a lot of duplication and make the review bigger.

But I at least wanted to get to a point where I wasn't making a bad problem worse.

OK, it looks like the native side is returning two things, 1) the EVP_MAC*, 2) whether or not the library even had the EVP_MAC_fetch function.

If the library doesn't have EVP_MAC_fetch then it doesn't have KMAC, so we'll return null and know there's no KMAC.  But if it does have EVP_MAC_fetch we expect the algorithm to be present, and if not, we throw.

Isn't that a problem if a) some distro or private build simply chose to build with KMAC disabled; or b) we try to use this routine for some algorithm introduced in the future?

Two extra variant tests of this come to mind (maybe I'll see them later):

1) Append part of the data, call GetCurrentHash to see that it's "wrong", then append the rest and see that it's "right" despite being inspected earlier.
2) After GetHashAndReset see that GetCurrentHash has changed.
I don't know if it should be on all the KATs, or something else special, but there should be tests for null/empty equivalency on the customization string.
